emit_cast_instrs_impl matches on CastKind, but the same three RISC-V extension sequences are typed out verbatim over and over inside the arms: 'slli t0,t0,56 / srai t0,t0,56' three times, 'slli 48 / srai 48' three times, 'slli 48 / srli 48' three times, 'slli 32 / srli 32' three times, 'andi t0,t0,0xff' four times and 'sext.w t0,t0' four times. Two helpers keyed on IrType, one sign-extending and one zero-extending or truncating, would serve the inner matches of FloatToSigned, FloatToUnsigned, SignedToFloat, SignedToUnsignedSameSize, IntWiden and IntNarrow and cut roughly a hundred lines to about twenty-five. The factoring is behavior-preserving and is the natural shape for a codegen backend.

emit_cast_instrs_impl repeats the same RISC-V extension idioms verbatim across six CastKind arms: slli/srai 56 for I8 appears in FloatToSigned, SignedToFloat, IntWiden and IntNarrow, slli/srli 48 for U16 in FloatToUnsigned, SignedToUnsignedSameSize, IntWiden and IntNarrow, and sext.w and andi t0,t0,0xff likewise three times each. Two helpers, emit_sign_extend_to(IrType) and emit_zero_extend_to(IrType), each carrying the IrType match once, would absorb the whole of SignedToUnsignedSameSize, IntWiden and IntNarrow and the tails of the two float-to-int arms, cutting well over half the 191 lines with no behavior change. The remaining fmv/fcvt pairs would then be the only per-arm content.

substitute_riscv_asm_operands is a hand-rolled character scanner taking nine parallel operand slices, and its while loop carries five independent branches: %z[name], %zN, %lo and %hi passthrough, %[name] and positional %N. The %z handling alone runs about 65 lines and duplicates the name lookup the %[name] branch performs, so both a helper per modifier and an operand struct are available.

substitute_riscv_asm_operands in src/backend/riscv/codegen/inline_asm.rs is one char cursor loop carrying seven separate branches: %%, the %z modifier with its own named and positional sublookups spanning about seventy lines, %lo, %hi, %[name], %N, and the passthrough. The %z[name] and %[name] lookups repeat the same op_names scan, so extracting a lookup helper plus one function per modifier removes both the length and the duplication.

combined_local_pass is one while loop carrying seven patterns that the module doc comment already enumerates by number and that the body already separates with '--- Pattern: ... ---' banners: self-move, reverse-move, redundant jump, conditional-branch inversion, adjacent store/load, redundant extension and redundant xorl. Each block reads only store, infos, i and len and signals its result through mark_nop plus 'changed', so each becomes a fn(store, &mut infos, i) -> bool, and the sixty-line rax_is_zero state machine becomes its own update function. That keeps the single linear scan the merge was written for, which is the only rationale the doc comment gives for the size.

combined_local_pass is documented as seven previously separate passes merged into one linear scan, and the body is exactly that: seven self-contained blocks (self-move, reverse-move, redundant jmp, cond-branch inversion, adjacent store/load, redundant extension, redundant xorl) each of which reads infos[i], calls mark_nop or replace_line, and ends with i += 1; continue. Only the xorl block and the rax_is_zero tracking match share mutable state; the other six touch nothing but store, infos, i and len. Each becomes a fn try_pattern(store, infos, i, len) -> bool called in sequence inside the same loop, which preserves the single-scan rationale the module header gives while dropping the function from 375 lines to a dispatch of seven calls.

Despite its name, types.rs holds three concerns: the LineInfo, LineKind, ExtKind and MoveSize declarations (lines 11 to 200), the classification pass (classify_line, classify_mov_ext, classify_arith_ext, about 320 lines), and roughly thirty free utilities including register_family_fast, REG_NAMES, scan_register_refs, memrchr and write_rbp_pattern. The peephole directory already has a passes subdirectory to model the split on.

src/backend/x86/codegen/peephole/types.rs stacks three concerns its own header names: the LineInfo, LineKind, ExtKind and MoveSize declarations, classify_line at 182 lines, and roughly thirty free helpers covering register naming (register_family_fast, reg_digit_to_id, reg_id_to_name), rbp parsing (parse_rbp_offset, parse_store_to_rbp_str), condition codes (parse_setcc, invert_cc) and byte formatting (write_u32_digits). The type declarations share no state with the parsers, so a types, classify and parse split is straightforward.

The file's own header says the parser is split into expressions.rs, types.rs, statements.rs, declarations.rs and declarators.rs, each adding pub(super) methods to Parser, yet parse.rs still carries three unrelated clusters beyond the Parser struct and parse(): the whole GCC __attribute__ family (parse_gcc_attribute_list, dispatch_gcc_attribute, and the cleanup/mode/vector_size/ext_vector_type/address_space handlers, lines 684-950), the pragma handling (handle_pragma_pack_token, handle_pragma_visibility_token), and the static sizeof/alignof type-spec helpers (try_sizeof_type_spec, alignof_type_spec, preferred_alignof_type_spec). Moving the attribute cluster alone to an attributes.rs impl block is mechanical under the convention the module already uses and takes the file well under a thousand lines.

The file's own header states the parser is split into focused modules (expressions.rs, types.rs, statements.rs, declarations.rs, declarators.rs), each adding an impl Parser block, and parse.rs then holds two slices that do not belong to core parsing: the GCC __attribute__ subsystem at lines 645 to 985 (parse_gcc_attributes, parse_gcc_attribute_list, dispatch_gcc_attribute, parse_string_attr_arg, parse_cleanup_attr, parse_mode_attr, parse_vector_size_attr, parse_ext_vector_type_attr, parse_address_space_attr, try_parse_asm_register_name) and the pragma handlers at 986 to 1075 (handle_pragma_pack_token, handle_pragma_visibility_token). Moving those into attributes.rs and pragmas.rs is the convention the directory already uses and removes roughly 430 of the 1308 lines without touching a call site, since the methods are pub(super).

The file mixes a 275-line parse_type_specifier flag collector with a separate struct, union and enum group (parse_struct_or_union, parse_struct_field_declarators, consume_struct_field_qualifiers, parse_enum_specifier) that runs about 300 lines and shares nothing but the Parser receiver. Sibling modules declarators.rs, statements.rs and expressions.rs show the parser is already split along exactly this kind of seam.

src/frontend/parser/types.rs carries one impl Parser whose parse_type_specifier alone spans 269 lines, plus separable groups for struct and union fields (parse_struct_fields, parse_struct_field_declarators, consume_struct_field_qualifiers), enums (parse_enum_specifier, parse_enum_variants, register_enum_constants), typeof, and abstract declarator suffixes. The file already lives in a parser directory, so moving the struct and enum groups into sibling modules needs no signature change.

try_lower_builtin_call is a chain of independent special cases before the final resolve_builtin dispatch: the user-definition override with its SSE exception, __builtin_choose_expr, the alloca match, the three-arm va_start/va_end/va_copy match, __builtin_expect, __builtin_prefetch, __builtin_unreachable and __builtin_trap. Each returns Option<Operand> and touches only self, name and args, so each extracts unchanged. The file already sets that precedent: lower_builtin_intrinsic sits right below it, extracted from the BuiltinKind::Intrinsic arm of this very function.

try_lower_builtin_call is a sequence of independent name-keyed blocks before the generic dispatch: __builtin_choose_expr, the alloca match, the three-arm va_start/va_end/va_copy match, __builtin_expect, __builtin_prefetch, __builtin_unreachable, __builtin_trap, then a delegation to try_lower_atomic_builtin and the resolve_builtin match. Each block already returns Option<Operand> and touches only self, name and args, so lower_choose_expr, lower_alloca_builtin and try_lower_va_builtin are direct lifts. The file itself demonstrates the pattern twice, with lower_builtin_intrinsic extracted for the Intrinsic arm and try_lower_atomic_builtin living in expr_atomics.rs, so the decomposition is the one the author already applied elsewhere.

lower_function_call runs sequential, independently testable phases: stripping no-op Deref layers, unwrapping AddressOf on a function name, resolving _Generic selections, dispatching __builtin_ and error-attribute functions, computing the sret and two-register return convention, lowering arguments with implicit casts and complex decomposition, then emitting the call. Each phase reads only the expression and produces one named value.

lower_function_call in src/ir/lowering/expr_calls.rs chains distinct stages: stripping Deref and AddressOf wrappers, resolving _Generic, builtin and error-function dispatch, classifying the sret and two-register return convention, lowering and decomposing arguments, a 35-line five-level-deep num_fixed_args computation over param_ctypes, the sret alloca prologue, then four post-call return paths. The file already hosts helpers such as unpack_two_reg_return, so pulling out the return convention and the variadic fixed-argument count follows the existing pattern.

structs.rs holds two responsibilities that never call into each other: type registration and layout computation (register_struct_type, register_nested_struct_types, recompute_vector_struct_layouts, struct_layout_key, union_layout_key, mark_transparent_union, lines 19-345) and member-access resolution (the resolve_member_access / resolve_member_access_full / resolve_member_access_with_ctype trio with their _impl bodies, get_layout_for_expr, resolve_field_struct_layout, resolve_func_call_struct_layout, lines 608-1050), with the 215-line get_struct_base_addr between them. The sibling lowering module is already split this way into twenty-five files by responsibility, including struct_init.rs for the initializer half, so a struct_access.rs split follows the crate's own convention rather than inventing one.

structs.rs holds two disjoint responsibilities in one impl Lowerer: type registration and layout computation at lines 19 to 271 (register_struct_type, recompute_vector_struct_layouts, recompute_layout_if_vector_fields, insert_struct_layout_scoped, invalidate_ctype_cache_scoped, register_nested_struct_types, struct_layout_key, union_layout_key, mark_transparent_union), then member-access resolution from 272 to 1050 (get_struct_base_addr, the six resolve_member_access variants, get_layout_for_expr, resolve_field_struct_layout, resolve_func_call_struct_layout). The two groups share only self.types.struct_layouts, and the lowering directory already carries forty files at exactly this granularity, including struct_init.rs, expr_access.rs and types_ctype.rs. Splitting into struct_layout.rs and struct_members.rs follows the established convention and cuts the file below the bound.

compute_decl_info returns a five-element tuple (alloc_size, elem_size, is_array, is_pointer, array_dim_strides) and branches into four self-contained size computations: simple or typedef pointer, array of pointers including the function-pointer-array dim ordering, pointer to array with its trailing-pointer counting, and the plain array or scalar case. Each branch is a nameable helper and the tuple is a struct waiting to be declared.

compute_decl_info in src/ir/lowering/types.rs returns a five-element tuple and branches into three independent cases: plain pointer, pointer combined with array (which itself splits into array-of-pointers with its last_ptr_pos dimension collection and pointer-to-array with its trailing_ptr_count analysis), and the remaining array case. Each branch computes its own sizes and strides from derived and resolved_ctype only, so one function per declarator shape is a direct extraction.

main is a match over roughly thirty Commands variants, and the arms are inconsistent: Epd, DumpBinpack and SplitBinpack are three-line delegations to epd::run_epd, run_dump_binpack and run_split_binpack, while EvalBench inlines about two hundred lines of NNUE loading, EPD parsing, warm-up and timing, Bench inlines the whole --set tunable parsing loop plus the multi-threaded spawn/join, and InspectBinpack, PatchNet and DumpThreats inline eighty to ninety lines each. Extracting run_eval_bench and its peers as free functions is exactly what the file already does for the binpack commands, and it takes main back to the dispatch it is supposed to be.

main is a clap match cli.command whose arms carry entire subcommand implementations inline: the Bench arm parses --set overrides, clamps against search::tunable_params, rebuilds the LMR table and spawns the thread pool in about seventy lines, and the EvalBench arm alone runs past three hundred, loading the NNUE net, building the position corpus, and branching over five bench modes (fresh, refresh, incremental, make-unmake, make-unmake-all) with their own accumulators and counters. Each arm reads only its own destructured fields plus cli.nnue, so lifting them to run_bench(...), run_eval_bench(...) and so on is mechanical and leaves main as the signal setup, the genfens intercept, the banner and a dispatch. Nothing about the 772 lines is forced.

movepicker.rs stacks four independent units plus tests: the History tables with their bonus and aging math (lines 21 to 186), the staged MovePicker itself (188 to 920), a 200-line is_pseudo_legal validator that touches no picker state, QMovePicker (1180 to 1326), and six separate test modules from line 1327 on. History and is_pseudo_legal are natural sibling files.

src/movepicker.rs stacks four unrelated units plus five test modules: the History table struct with its scoring and aging methods, the staged MovePicker with generate_and_score_captures, quiets and evasions, a standalone is_pseudo_legal validator of 200 lines, and QMovePicker. The pseudo-legality checker touches no picker state and already has three test modules devoted to it, so moving history and pseudo_legal into sibling files is a clean cut.

export_html interleaves three separable things in one body: an 85-line CSS raw-string literal, a 30-line navigation JavaScript raw-string literal, and the per-slide render loop whose six sections (title/subtitle, bullets, code blocks, block quotes, tables, image data-URI, notes) each push into the same String. Hoisting the two literals to consts and lifting the loop body to fn render_slide(&Slide) -> String leaves the entry point at roughly forty lines with no behavior change, since the only shared state is the html accumulator. Nothing here is forced by a trait contract; escape_html already sits beside it as a free helper.

export_html holds about 115 lines of embedded asset text (the :root/@media print CSS block and the showSlide keydown script) that are pure constants with only four interpolated theme colors, plus a per-slide loop that emits eight distinct element kinds (title, subtitle, bullets, code blocks, blockquotes, tables, base64 image, notes) including the fs::read plus extension-to-MIME match for the image. Hoisting the two literals to const CSS_TEMPLATE and const NAV_SCRIPT and lifting the loop body to render_slide(&mut String, &Slide), with the data-URI work in its own helper, leaves the entry point at roughly thirty lines. Nothing here is forced by a trait contract or by output ordering.

apply_font_change bundles two independent strategies plus a resize drain: the slide path builds a full-screen buffer, computes Kitty font stepping parameters, and runs a dissolve loop nested five levels deep (frame, row, span, char, cell padding) while interleaving font step batches, and the plain path then switches on font_capability. The dissolve frame renderer alone is an obvious extraction.

apply_font_change in src/render/engine/font.rs nests the whole scatter-dissolve renderer inside its slide-transition branch: a per-row, per-span, per-char loop computing dimmed colors and a hash threshold, six levels deep, followed by Kitty font step batching, frame pacing, and then the plain stepping path and the resize drain. Extracting render_dissolve_frame and a font stepping helper leaves the top level as the phase sequence it already describes in its doc comment.

create_tpcc_schema_vibesql is nine consecutive db.create_table(TableSchema::with_primary_key(...)).unwrap() statements for warehouse, district, customer, history, new_order, orders, order_line, item and stock, with no branching, no loop and no state beyond the varchar() closure. The length is the arity of the TPC-C schema itself, about ninety ColumnSchema::new lines whose column names and types all differ, so there is nothing to factor and a split into nine single-statement functions would add indirection without removing anything. The flat declarative sequence is the clearest form and matches the sibling MySQL schema function in the same file.

create_tpcc_schema_vibesql is nine db.create_table(TableSchema::with_primary_key(...)) calls, one per TPC-C table, and every line inside them is a ColumnSchema::new literal transcribed from the benchmark specification: no branch, no loop, no local state beyond the varchar() closure that already removes the one repeated piece of scaffolding. The 229 lines are the size of the fixed TPC-C schema, and the declaration order (warehouse, district, customer, history, new_order, orders, order_line, item, stock) is the order the standard defines, which is what makes the block readable against the spec. Breaking it into nine one-call functions would add nine names and nine indirections without making any of the column lists shorter or clearer.

The TableSchema impl runs 45 methods across four unrelated groups: six with_* builder constructors (with_primary_key through with_all_constraint_types), read accessors (get_column, column_count, primary_key_effective_collations), column mutations (add_column, remove_column, rename_column, set_column_nullable, set_column_default), and constraint mutations (add and drop for check, unique and foreign key). Splitting into per-concern impl blocks changes no call site.

The TableSchema impl in crates/vibesql-catalog/src/table.rs carries about forty methods in four clear groups: builders (with_primary_key, with_unique_constraints, with_foreign_keys, with_all_constraints, with_all_constraint_types, with_storage_format), plain accessors, column mutation (add_column, remove_column, rename_column, set_column_nullable, set_column_default), and constraint mutation (add and drop for check, unique and foreign key). Rust allows an inherent impl to be split across files, so each group can move without touching a single call site.

process_constraints is two independent phases against one accumulator: the column-level loop matching ColumnConstraintKind over roughly a hundred and ten lines, then the table-level loop matching TableConstraintKind over sixty-five, sharing only `result` and the has_column_level_pk flag that the first phase alone owns. Each phase extracts to a function taking table_name, columns and &mut ConstraintResult, and each keeps its own exhaustive match, so no compile-time coverage is lost. The file already hosts free helpers of that shape next door: dedup_pk_key_parts, key_part_collations and validate_check_expression.

process_constraints is two independent loops over two disjoint vocabularies, ColumnConstraintKind (nine arms) and TableConstraintKind (five arms), sharing only the ConstraintResult accumulator and the MultiplePrimaryKeys error. Extracting apply_column_constraint(&mut result, table_name, col_def, constraint) and apply_table_constraint(&mut result, table_name, columns, table_constraint) is a mechanical split, and the CHECK handling is currently duplicated word for word between them: validate_check_expression(expr) followed by name.clone().or_else(|| source_text.clone()).unwrap_or_else(|| expr.to_sql()), which one helper would serve for both. The file already hosts free helpers of this shape (key_part_collations, dedup_pk_key_parts, validate_check_expression), so the factoring matches its own conventions.

check_child_references_impl is two phases joined by one vector: a 140-line collection loop over every catalog table and each of its foreign keys, extracting parent key values and scanning the child table under an MVCC snapshot, followed by a 100-line dispatch matching Restrict, NoAction, Cascade, SetNull and SetDefault. The intermediate actions_to_perform tuple is already the seam between them.

check_child_references_impl in crates/vibesql-executor/src/delete/integrity.rs is two phases joined by a five-element tuple vector: a nested scan over every catalog table and each of its foreign keys that resolves parent indices, filters NULL keys and probes the child table with scan_visible, then a second loop matching ReferentialAction to raise, cascade or queue. Collecting the actions and applying them are independent and share only actions_to_perform, so the split is direct.

hash_expression is a single exhaustive match over the ~40 variants of vibesql_ast::Expression, and every arm is variant-specific field enumeration (ColumnRef hashes table_canonical/column_canonical, Between hashes expr/low/high/negated/symmetric, MatchAgainst hashes columns then search_modifier then mode). There is no repeated scaffold to factor: the length is exactly the number of AST variants times the fields each one carries. Splitting it into hash_subquery/hash_temporal groups would force the outer arms to keep naming the variants and then re-match inside, and would give up the one place where the compiler's exhaustiveness check catches a newly added Expression variant.

hash_expression is one exhaustive match over roughly forty Expression variants, each arm two to eight lines hashing that variant's own fields (Case walks when_clauses, Between hashes five members, the subquery arms hash a Debug string). There is no shared scaffold to factor: no two arms repeat the same shape, so a split could only group variants behind delegating sub-functions that re-match with a catch-all, which is exactly the guarantee the current form buys, since adding a variant to Expression today forces an edit here. The length is the size of the AST, not a decomposition the maintainers declined.

eval_between opens with three dispatch prologues (row value constructor operands, scalar subquery against row-value bounds, the mixed row-value misuse check), then defines a 35-line transform_for_collation closure handling NOCASE and RTRIM over four SqlValue variants, then runs affinity resolution and the reversed-bounds and negation comparisons. The collation transform is a pure function that belongs beside the other collation helpers.

eval_between in crates/vibesql-executor/src/evaluator/expressions/predicates.rs opens with three dispatch prologues (row value constructors, a scalar subquery against row-value bounds, and the RowValueMisused guard), then defines transform_for_collation as a 25-line closure duplicating NOCASE and RTRIM handling per SqlValue variant, then handles reversed bounds, affinity and the three-valued result. The collation transform is a pure function that belongs beside the collation module, and the row-value prologue is already delegating.

deserialize_value's bulk is mechanical boilerplate, not dispatch: the INTEGER, SMALLINT, BIGINT, UNSIGNED, NUMERIC, FLOAT, REAL and DOUBLE arms are eight copies of `let mut buf = [0u8; N]; reader.read_exact(&mut buf)?; Ok(...::from_le_bytes(buf))`, and CHARACTER/VARCHAR, INTERVAL, VECTOR and BLOB each re-spell the same `read u32 length, then read that many bytes` prologue. A `read_le::<N>(reader)` helper and a `read_len_prefixed(reader)` helper collapse those twelve arms to one or two lines each and take the function well under the bound, leaving the tag dispatch itself untouched. The DATE and TIMESTAMP arms, which carry the real logic (the from_parts_unchecked leniency comment), also stop being buried in byte plumbing.

deserialize_value repeats one scaffold nine times over: `let mut buf = [0u8; N]; reader.read_exact(&mut buf)?; Ok(SqlValue::X(T::from_le_bytes(buf)))` for INTEGER, SMALLINT, BIGINT, UNSIGNED, NUMERIC, FLOAT, REAL and DOUBLE, and a second one three times for the u32 length-prefixed payloads of CHARACTER/VARCHAR, INTERVAL and BLOB. A `read_le<const N: usize>` helper and a `read_len_prefixed(reader)` helper collapse those twelve arms to one line each, and the DATE and TIMESTAMP arms share the year/month/day and hour/minute/second/nano readers verbatim. The factoring is mechanical and behavior-preserving.

try_extract_subqueries_to_joins carries two blocks of about 45 lines each, one for the left operand and one for the right of the And arm, that repeat the same In, Exists and scalar-comparison dispatch with only the sibling expression swapped, followed by two more symmetric recursive branches. One helper taking the candidate side and its remainder collapses all four.

try_extract_subqueries_to_joins in crates/vibesql-executor/src/optimizer/subquery_to_join/mod.rs repeats the same 45-line In, Exists and scalar-comparison dispatch three times: once for the left side of a BinaryOp And, once for the right side with only the retained operand swapped, and a third time inside the Conjunction arm. One helper taking the candidate child and the surviving predicate folds all three.

The 2268 lines carry no test module at all: it is all production code, and it holds at least four independent concerns that already sit in contiguous runs. Table-reference discovery (collect_stmt_table_refs, collect_from_table_refs, collect_expr_table_refs at 724-1038 plus stmt_references_table, from_clause_references_table, expr_references_table at 2137-2268), wildcard expansion (WildcardColumn, WildcardSource, visible_columns, view_column_names, expand_wildcard_names, collect_from_sources, collect_select_list_columns at 1096-1371) and the recursive-CTE machinery (RecursiveSplit, split_recursive_compound, execute_recursive_cte, execute_recursive_frontier, execute_recursive_queue at 1371-1980) each move to a cte/refs.rs, cte/wildcard.rs and cte/recursive.rs with no signature change, leaving execute_ctes and execute_cte_at in the parent.

cte.rs is 2268 lines of production code with no test module, holding about forty free functions in four disjoint groups: CTE scheduling (execute_ctes, execute_cte_list, execute_cte_at, execute_cte_body, CteState), dependency analysis (compute_needed_ctes, collect_stmt_table_refs, collect_from_table_refs, collect_expr_table_refs), wildcard and schema expansion (cte_pseudo_schema, legacy_cte_schema, WildcardColumn, expand_wildcard_names, collect_from_sources, collect_select_list_columns) and the recursive machinery (RecursiveSplit, split_recursive_compound, execute_recursive_cte, execute_recursive_frontier, execute_recursive_queue, resolve_recursive_order_indices), lines 1533 to 2200. Those groups share no state beyond the function arguments, so a `cte/recursive.rs` and `cte/wildcard.rs` split is a file move.

evaluate is a single 569-line match over Expression whose arms are fully independent: Cast recurses then calls cast_value, Between reimplements symmetric bound swapping and three-valued logic, InList runs its own NULL bookkeeping loop, and Like re-derives text coercion across the SqlValue variants. Each arm is 50 to 150 lines and depends only on its own sub-expressions, so one function per arm is the direct decomposition.

evaluate in crates/vibesql-executor/src/select/executor/aggregation/evaluation/simple.rs is a single match of about thirteen arms whose bodies are self-contained: BETWEEN with its symmetric swap and three-valued combination runs 70 lines, LIKE with its text coercion and ESCAPE validation runs 135, GLOB another 90, plus IN list, POSITION, TRIM, INTERVAL, EXTRACT, Conjunction and Disjunction. Each arm reads only its own sub-expressions, group_rows and the evaluator, so one function per predicate is a mechanical lift.

execute_with_iterators is already written as labeled stages and the seams are named in its own comments: the ExecutionContext assembly (outer_row/procedural/trigger/cte/outer_rows, ~25 lines), Stage 2's five-arm WhereOptimization match, Stage 3 and 4's OFFSET/LIMIT boxing, and Stage 6's SIMD-or-row-by-row projection (~40 lines). Each is a self-contained extraction over values it already computes (schema, evaluator, filtered_rows), for instance a build_evaluation_context(&self, &schema) -> Evaluator and a project_rows(&self, &filtered_rows, stmt, &evaluator, &schema). Nothing here is forced by a trait contract; the function is long because six pipeline stages were inlined into one body.

execute_with_iterators is a linear six-stage pipeline whose stages are already labelled in comments and separable by their inputs. The ExecutionContext assembly (outer_row/procedural/trigger/cte/outer_rows, about 25 lines) depends only on `self` and the schema; the WhereOptimization match with its four arms building FilterIterator is about 40 lines keyed only on the iterator and the resolved predicate; the OFFSET/LIMIT block boxing `skip` and `take` is another 25. Extracting build_evaluator_context, apply_where_filter and apply_limit_offset leaves the entry point as the pipeline it documents itself to be, and none of the three would change behavior.

extract_column_refs is an exhaustive visitor over the Expression enum: every arm is one to three recursive calls, and the tail lists the terminal variants (Literal, Wildcard, CurrentDate, Placeholder and friends) explicitly with no wildcard arm. The length is set by the width of the AST, not by logic, and splitting the match would surrender the exhaustiveness check that forces every new variant to be handled.

extract_column_refs in crates/vibesql-executor/src/select/executor/validation/column_refs.rs is an exhaustive match over the Expression enum where nearly every arm is one to five lines of recursion into its children, and the terminal arms are a single grouped pattern listing Literal, Wildcard, CurrentDate, the placeholders and the rest. Its length tracks the variant count, and splitting it would break the exhaustiveness check that makes the compiler flag a newly added variant.

The twelve arms of resolve_aliases_in_expression repeat one concrete scaffold: call resolve_alias_or_clone on each child, set an any_resolved flag, then rebuild the variant with unwrap_or_else(|| child.as_ref().clone()) on every unresolved child, else return None. Between spends 20 lines on three children, InList and Function spend 20 more each on the same flag-tracking closure, and Case spends 60. A single `fn resolve_child(child, select_list, any: &mut bool) -> Expression` returning the clone when nothing resolved reduces every one of those arms to a two- to five-line rebuild and removes the hand-written flag bookkeeping that is currently duplicated in five closures.

encode_neon_float_two_misc and encode_neon_float_cmp_zero have the same signature, the same arrangement match (2s/4s/2d), the same size computation and the same word layout; only the error-message text differs. encode_neon_float_two_misc and encode_neon_float_cmp_zero take the same (u_bit, size_hi, opcode) parameters, accept the same 2s/4s/2d arrangements and build the same 0 Q U 01110 size 10000 opcode 10 Rn Rd word; only the error text differs. f128_flip_sign_bit is a trait method implemented once per backend: the ARM version emits mov/eor/mov on v0.d[1], the RISC-V version emits li/slli/xor on a1. The bodies are three self.state.emit calls whose entire content is the architecture-specific assembly literal, which the normalizer erases; there is no shared scaffold to factor between two backends the trait deliberately keeps apart. A minimal crate with two impls of one trait, each method making three emit calls with different string literals, would reproduce this misjudgment as a regression seed.

f128_flip_sign_bit is a per-backend trait method: the AArch64 version moves v0.d[1] to x0, XORs the sign bit and reinserts it, while the RISC-V version builds the mask in t0 and XORs a1. The bodies match only because both are three self.state.emit calls whose entire difference is the normalized asm string literals, so nothing remains to factor. A minimal crate with two impls of one trait, each emitting three different string literals, would reproduce this as a regression seed.

encode_cmpxchg and encode_xadd are line-for-line identical: same operand-count check, same size suffix, same (Register, Memory) match with the 0x66 prefix, emit_rex_rm, 0x0F escape and encode_modrm_mem; they differ only in the opcode pair (0xB0/0xB1 vs 0xC0/0xC1) and the mnemonic in error strings. One helper taking the mnemonic name and the two opcode bytes would serve both without changing the emitted bytes.

encode_cmpxchg and encode_xadd are line-for-line identical: same operand-count check, same size suffix, same reg-to-memory match arm emitting the 0x66 prefix, REX, a 0x0F-prefixed opcode and the ModRM; they differ only in the opcode pair (B0/B1 vs C0/C1) and the mnemonic in the error strings. One encoder taking the opcode base and name serves both.

add_weight_rows_avx2 and add_weight_rows_avx512 are per-ISA SIMD kernels under different #[target_feature] attributes; the doc comment on the AVX-512 one states it mirrors the AVX2 one by design. Every operation differs in the erased names: __m256i vs __m512i, _mm256_loadu/cvtepi8/add/storeu vs their _mm512 counterparts, 16 vs 32 lanes per register. Merging them would need a macro parameterized over roughly eight intrinsics and types in a hot path, which obscures each kernel for no behavioral gain. A minimal crate with two #[target_feature] functions differing only in intrinsic names and a lane-width literal would reproduce this misjudgment as a regression seed.

add_weight_rows_avx2 and add_weight_rows_avx512 are per-ISA SIMD kernels under different #[target_feature] attributes, using __m256i vs __m512i, different load, convert, add and store intrinsics and 16 vs 32 lanes per register; the doc comment states the AVX-512 one mirrors the AVX2 one by design. Every difference lives in the erased intrinsic names and lane literals, and unifying them would need a macro parameterized over intrinsics in a hot kernel. A minimal crate with two target_feature functions sharing a loop shape over different intrinsics could reproduce this as a regression seed.

BenchStats::print in vibesql-bench-common and in vibesql-storage/benches/harness.rs are identical, and the bench file's header says it is a simplified copy of the shared harness, with from_times and BenchConfig copied too. vibesql-bench-common is the workspace's shared benchmark crate and its default features pull only rand, so vibesql-storage could take it as a dev-dependency and use the one definition. crates/vibesql-storage/benches/harness.rs describes itself as a simplified version of the shared harness, and its BenchStats::print (with the stats computation above it) is a verbatim copy of vibesql-bench-common's, whose output format must stay compatible with the benchmark parsers. vibesql-bench-common has no default features and pulls only rand at default, so the storage benches could take it as a dev-dependency and drop the copy without changing behavior.

The two update_state methods share a now-in-millis computation and the terminal-state match, but the rest is store-specific SQL: profiling_sessions sets ended_at only, while sessions also maintains updated_at, so the statements and parameter lists differ in arity on both branches. What would be factored is a four-line timestamp idiom and a one-line predicate; a shared update_state would need two SQL strings and differently-sized params, which adds indirection to two parallel stores that have already diverged in schema. A minimal crate with two functions of identical control flow whose only differences are SQL literals and params arity would reproduce this misjudgment, since literal normalization hides the part that carries the semantics.

The two update_state methods belong to stores over different tables with different schemas: the session store also writes updated_at and binds now twice, while the profiling store writes only state and ended_at. What is shared is a four-line millisecond timestamp and a one-line terminal-state matches!, and the SQL that makes up the substance of each method has already diverged, so one definition would have to take the table and the column set as parameters. A minimal crate with two structs whose update methods share a timestamp prelude but issue different SQL could reproduce this as a regression seed.

encode_cset and encode_csetm share the whole body: parse rd, parse the condition operand, invert it, and assemble the conditional-select word with XZR in Rn and Rm. One helper taking op and o2 (shared with the csel/csinc/csinv/csneg family) would serve both without changing any encoding.

The two parse_instruction functions live in the AArch64 and RISC-V assembler parsers and each builds its own module's AsmStatement and calls its own parse_operands, which in RISC-V takes the mnemonic as a second argument. The two parse_instruction functions belong to separate per-ISA assembler parsers: each builds its own module's AsmStatement and calls its own parse_operands, and the RISC-V one already takes the mnemonic because operand parsing there depends on it. emit_i128_neg_impl exists once per backend: ARM emits mvn/mvn/adds/adc, RISC-V emits not/not/addi/seqz/add. emit_i128_neg_impl emits target-specific instruction sequences: AArch64 uses mvn/mvn/adds/adc, RISC-V uses not/not/addi/seqz/add to propagate the carry by hand. emit_jcc_block, emit_instr_imm and emit_instr_rbp are #[inline] fast-path emitters that each push a fixed shape into the buffer without format!: they differ in the separator literals (" .LBB", " $", "(%rbp)"), in which integer writer they call (write_u64_fast vs write_i64_fast) and in operand order. Each body is four or five push calls; the difference lives entirely in literals and callee names, and a shared helper would just be a format string interpreter undoing the reason they exist. emit_jcc_block, emit_instr_reg and emit_instr_rbp are #[inline] fast-path writers into the assembly buffer, each spelling out one AT&T operand syntax (.LBB label, %reg, offset(%rbp)) through a few push_str and write_*_fast calls. The shared shape is the push_str/newline idiom itself, and the differences (operand sigil, integer writer, suffix) are the whole point of each method, so a generic helper would be no shorter and would obscure the emitted syntax. emit_int_cmp_impl in the i686 and x86-64 backends share the same ten-arm IrCmpOp to setcc mnemonic table and the same set/zero-extend/invalidate/store tail; they differ only in the compare prelude and the eax vs rax register names. The repository has src/backend/x86_common.rs whose header states it exists to share condition code mappings between exactly these two backends, so moving the IrCmpOp-to-setcc table there is a change the project's own design asks for, with no behavior change.

Both emit_int_cmp_impl functions carry the same ten-arm IrCmpOp to setcc mnemonic table (sete through setae), which is common to both x86-family targets; only the compare prelude (cmpl vs width-typed) and the zero-extend/store epilogue (eax vs rax) differ. The same mapping recurs in the jcc variants in both comparison.rs files, so one shared condition-code function in the backend crate serves both without changing behavior, and the prelude and epilogue stay per-target.

encode_alu_reg, encode_fp_sgnj and encode_fmv_x_f are four-line RISC-V encoders that already delegate the word layout to the shared encode_r; what remains is fetching operands with the register-class getter the format requires (get_reg vs get_freg), the opcode constant (OP_OP vs OP_OP_FP) and a fixed funct3. encode_alu_reg, encode_fp_sgnj and encode_fmv_x_f are three- to four-line instruction-format encoders that each fetch operands with the right register class (get_reg vs get_freg, two or three operands) and delegate to the shared encode_r with a different opcode. The shared encoding already lives in encode_r, and what differs (register classes, opcode, fixed funct3) is the substance of each encoder. A minimal crate with several short functions that fetch typed operands and call one shared packer could reproduce this as a regression seed.

encode_v_arith_vx and encode_v_arith_vi are the OPIVX and OPIVI encoders: they differ exactly in what the format distinguishes, the third operand (scalar register via get_reg vs 5-bit immediate via get_imm masked to 0x1F) and funct3 (100 vs 011). encode_v_arith_vx and encode_v_arith_vi are the scalar-register and immediate forms of RVV OPIVX/OPIVI: one reads an integer register with get_reg, the other a 5-bit immediate with get_imm masked to 0x1F, and they set different funct3 values (100 vs 011). Each is a five-line format encoder whose doc comment gives its bit layout; factoring the single packing expression would not shrink anything and would obscure the per-format layout. A minimal crate with two five-line bit-packing functions differing in one operand fetch and one constant could reproduce this as a regression seed.

emit_fused_cmp_branch_impl and emit_fused_cmp_branch_blocks_impl share the same use_32bit computation, the same emit_int_cmp_insn_typed call and the same ten-arm IrCmpOp to jcc table (the second one only prefixes each mnemonic with four spaces), then differ in emitting to labels vs block ids. emit_fused_cmp_branch_impl and emit_fused_cmp_branch_blocks_impl share the use_32bit compare prelude and the full ten-arm IrCmpOp to jcc table (the second just prefixes each mnemonic with four spaces), and differ only in whether they emit jumps to labels or to block ids. handle_if and handle_elif run the same five-step #if expression pipeline: resolve_defined_in_expr, expand_line_reuse, resolve_defined_in_expr again, replace_remaining_idents_with_zero and evaluate_condition; they differ only in the last call (push_if vs handle_elif). handle_if and handle_elif run the same four-step condition pipeline (resolve defined/__has_*, expand macros, resolve again, replace remaining identifiers with zero, evaluate_condition) and differ only in the final call, push_if vs handle_elif; the elif comment even says 'same reason as handle_if'. That double-resolve ordering is subtle enough that a fix to one must be mirrored in the other, so an evaluate_if_expr(&mut self, expr) -> bool helper would plausibly be accepted.

read_u8 and read_u16 are three-line binary readers that differ in the return type, the buffer size and the conversion (buf[0] vs u16::from_le_bytes). read_u8 and read_u16 are three-line binary readers that differ in buffer width, return type and decoding (buf[0] vs u16::from_le_bytes), with read_u32 following the same pattern. One small helper per width is the clearest available form for a weight-file reader, and a generic or macro version would be longer than what it replaces. visit_statement in the executor's bind/visitor.rs re-declares the same ClosureVisitor struct, the same ExpressionVisitor and StatementVisitor impls and the same walk_statement call as vibesql_ast::visitor::visit_expressions; the only difference is holding &mut F instead of F. load_lineitem_sqlite and load_lineitem_duckdb repeat the full TPC-H lineitem generation: the order/line loop, part and supplier key formulas, quantity, price, discount, tax, three random dates and the flag/mode selections; they differ only in the connection type and rusqlite::params! vs duckdb::params!. The members are not a comparison pair of the code under measurement but data loaders whose generated rows must be identical across engines for the comparison to be fair, so a shared row generator (iterator yielding the computed fields, consumed by each engine) would serve both without changing behavior and remove a drift risk.

load_lineitem_sqlite and load_lineitem_duckdb repeat the same 40-line LINEITEM row generator (the order/line loops, the part/supplier key derivation, the quantity, price, discount, tax and date formulas, the flag and ship-mode picks), and differ only in the connection type and rusqlite::params! vs duckdb::params!. map_branch_conjunct and map_conjunct are the same 120-line whitelist rewriter over Expression; the branch version's doc comment says it mirrors map_conjunct, and the only differences are the context type (BranchPushContext vs PushContext, both exposing resolve_column) and comments. A small trait with resolve_column, or one generic function, serves both and removes the risk that a safety arm added to one whitelist is missed in the other.

string_to_truthy in select/executor/arena_execution.rs is the same SQLite string-to-boolean conversion as string_to_truthy in select/filter.rs, statement for statement, minus comments and with map/unwrap_or in place of a match. Both are private functions in the same crate, so making one pub(crate) and calling it from the other serves both without changing behavior and keeps one definition of a SQLite semantics rule.

arena_execution.rs carries its own string_to_truthy that duplicates select/filter.rs's string_to_truthy in the same crate: same empty and trim checks, same sign handling, same numeric-prefix scan and f64 parse, differing only in using unwrap_or(false) instead of a match. This SQLite truthiness rule must agree everywhere it is applied, so one pub(crate) definition should serve both.

parse_expression_sql and parse_alter_table_sql both build a Lexer, call tokenize() with the identical map_err closure formatting "Lexer error: {}", and construct ArenaParser::new(tokens, arena); they differ only in the final parser method called (and the arena.alloc wrap). The same lex-and-construct scaffold is copied into more than a dozen sibling entry points in this impl (parse_insert, parse_update, parse_delete, parse_replace and their _with_interner variants). One private helper returning the ready ArenaParser would serve every member without changing behavior, so the repeated error-mapping scaffold is worth factoring.

parse_expression_sql and parse_alter_table_sql both build a Lexer, tokenize with the same map_err formatting "Lexer error: {}", construct ArenaParser::new and then call one parse method; the only differences are the method called and the arena.alloc wrap on the expression result. The same three-statement setup recurs in parse_insert, parse_update, parse_delete, parse_replace and the four *_with_interner variants in this file, so the scaffold is repeated, not a one-off delegation. One helper returning a tokenized ArenaParser (or taking the parse step as a closure) would serve every entry point without changing behavior.

Deserialize for Level and Deserialize for LevelFilter each define an identifier Visitor (expecting, visit_u64, visit_str, visit_bytes), a DeserializeSeed impl, and an enum Visitor with visit_enum, about 75 lines each with the same control flow. The only differences are the target type, the expecting string, and whether the names slice is LOG_LEVEL_NAMES[1..] or LOG_LEVEL_NAMES. Both types implement FromStr, so one generic visitor parameterized by the names slice and expecting text (or a small macro) would serve both impls without changing behavior; the duplicated scaffold is nontrivial, not a short delegation.

Deserialize for Level and Deserialize for LevelFilter are 75-line bodies that are line-for-line the same: an identifier Visitor with visit_u64/visit_str/visit_bytes, a DeserializeSeed impl, an enum Visitor with visit_enum, and a deserialize_enum call. They differ only in the target type, the expecting string, the enum name and whether LOG_LEVEL_NAMES is sliced from 1. The trait impls must stay separate, but their bodies are a nontrivial shared scaffold that one macro_rules! (or a generic helper parameterized over the type, name and name slice) could generate without changing behavior.

The three members are the Flag::update methods of the CaseSensitive, Files and TypeList flag structs: each is an assert on v.unwrap_switch(), a single field assignment (args.case = CaseMode::Sensitive, args.mode.update(Mode::Files), args.mode.update(Mode::Types)), and Ok(()). The bodies are three lines whose entire difference is which field is set, and each lives in a separate trait impl that ripgrep's flag design requires per flag; there is no scaffold to factor. A minimal crate with one trait and three impls whose short method bodies differ only in the assigned field could reproduce this as a regression seed.

The three members are Flag::update for CaseSensitive, Files and TypeList: each is an assert on v.unwrap_switch() followed by a single assignment to a different LowArgs field or Mode, then Ok(()). Each sits in its own impl Flag block, which ripgrep's per-flag design and the trait force apart, and the whole difference is the field and value assigned. Nothing nontrivial is left to factor, because a shared helper would just restate the trait method. A minimal crate with one trait implemented on three unit structs whose three-line method bodies differ only in the assigned field reproduces this, so it can serve as a regression seed.

The members are the Flag::update impls for LineNumber, NoConfig and NullData: an assert on v.unwrap_switch() with a message, one or two field assignments (args.line_number = Some(true), args.no_config = true, args.crlf = false plus args.null_data = true), then Ok(()). Each is a separate trait impl the flag registry requires, and the bodies are too short to share anything beyond the trait signature; the difference lives entirely in the fields written. A minimal crate with several trait impls whose three-line bodies assign different fields could reproduce this as a regression seed.

LineNumber::update, NoConfig::update and NullData::update are each an unwrap_switch assert plus one or two field assignments on LowArgs (line_number, no_config, crlf/null_data) inside separate impl Flag blocks. The similarity comes entirely from the trait method signature and the assert idiom, and the difference is exactly the semantic assignment. Separate trait impls the language forces apart leave nothing to factor here. This is reproducible as a regression seed with a minimal crate in which several unit structs implement one trait method as an assert followed by a distinct field write.

shr and shl are mirrored five-line primitives on ExtendedFloat: shr does fp.mant >>= shift and fp.exp += shift, shl does fp.mant <<= shift and fp.exp -= shift, each with a debug_assert bound. The whole difference is the shift direction and the sign of the exponent update, which are exactly what the normalization treats as near-equal; merging them behind a direction parameter would obscure two textbook operations and add a branch on a hot inline path. A minimal crate with a paired shift-left/shift-right helper differing only in operators could reproduce this as a regression seed.

shr and shl are four-statement primitives: compute the u64 bit width, debug_assert the shift bound, then fp.mant >>= shift; fp.exp += shift versus fp.mant <<= shift; fp.exp -= shift. The whole difference lies in the operators and the assert message, which together are the semantics of each function, so a merged function with a direction parameter would be less clear and would add a branch to an #[inline] hot helper. They are mirror operations by design (adapted from rust-lexical). A minimal crate with two mirrored three-line functions that differ only in shift and sign operators reproduces this, so it can serve as a regression seed.

Deserialize for Number defines a NumberVisitor with visit_i64, visit_i128, visit_u64, visit_u128, visit_f64 and a cfg-gated visit_map, then calls deserialize_any; Deserialize for &RawValue defines a ReferenceVisitor with only visit_map ending in next_value_seed(ReferenceFromString), then calls deserialize_newtype_struct(TOKEN, ...). What they share is the serde Visitor boilerplate the trait contract imposes plus the RawKey/NumberKey map-key check, and they deserialize different types through different Deserializer entry points, so there is no common definition that would serve both. A minimal crate with two Deserialize impls whose local visitors share the serde skeleton, one a superset of the other, could probably reproduce this as a regression seed.

Deserialize for Number defines a NumberVisitor with visit_i64, visit_i128, visit_u64, visit_u128, visit_f64 and a feature-gated visit_map, then calls deserialize_any. Deserialize for &RawValue defines a ReferenceVisitor with only visit_map, which hands off to next_value_seed(ReferenceFromString), and calls deserialize_newtype_struct. Apart from the serde visitor boilerplate (expecting, the RawKey/NumberKey check in visit_map), the two share no logic: they are separate trait impls for different types with different visitor method sets and entry points, so nothing could be factored without changing behavior. A minimal crate with two Deserialize impls whose local Visitor structs share only the expecting/visit_map skeleton but differ in length reproduces this, so it can serve as a regression seed.

generation.rs mixes three separable responsibilities: per-function analysis prepasses (build_gep_fold_map, build_global_addr_map, build_foldable_global_addr_set, build_global_addr_ptr_set, count_value_uses, detect_cmp_branch_fusion, roughly lines 52 to 487), module-level emission (generate_module and the emit_* section helpers), and function/instruction dispatch (generate_function, generate_instruction, generate_terminator). The analysis helpers take only an IrFunction and return maps, so moving them to a sibling module is mechanical and matches how the backend is already split into many files. The file is not data-like, and the split would plausibly be accepted.

generation.rs holds three separable layers: the pre-codegen analyses (build_gep_fold_map, build_global_addr_map, build_foldable_global_addr_set, build_global_addr_ptr_set, count_value_uses, detect_cmp_branch_fusion, roughly lines 30-487), module-level emission (generate_module through emit_init_fini_arrays), and per-function/instruction dispatch (generate_function, which alone is about 200 lines, plus generate_instruction). The analyses are pure functions over IrFunction with no shared state, so moving them to a sibling module is mechanical. The backend already uses a split layout (liveness, common, traits), so a reviewer would plausibly accept this decomposition.

The 1062-line parser.rs holds the AST type definitions (Operand, DataValue, Directive, AsmStatement, lines 19 to 186), a directive parser with its section/type/size/data-value helpers (parse_directive through parse_symbol_addend, lines 325 to 772), and the instruction/operand parser (parse_instruction through parse_int_literal, lines 773 onward). These are independent seams connected only through the AST types, so moving the types or the directive parsing to a sibling file is straightforward and would bring the file under the threshold. The file is barely over the bound, but the split is clean and conventional for an assembler front end.

The RISC-V parser.rs mixes the statement/AST type definitions, the directive parser (parse_directive is about 200 lines) with its data-value helpers (parse_data_values, strip_outer_parens, parse_single_data_value, parse_symbol_addend) and the instruction/operand parser. The directive and data-value half is architecture-generic and has counterparts in the x86 and ARM parsers, and the crate already has backend::asm_preprocess as a shared home for such helpers. Splitting directives and operands into submodules is a mechanical move along existing function boundaries and would plausibly be accepted.

This impl block is already the intrinsic-emission slice of X86Codegen split into its own file; it holds four small helpers and emit_intrinsic_impl, whose ~430 lines are one exhaustive match over the IntrinsicOp enum. Each arm is a short instruction sequence (fences, SSE binary ops, CRC32, AES-NI, scalar sqrt/fabs) and the repetitive arms already delegate to emit_sse_binary_128 and similar helpers. Splitting the block further would scatter one cohesive dispatch table across files without separating responsibilities. A minimal crate with an impl block dominated by one long match over an enum with short arms could reproduce this as a regression seed.

Extending that pattern to the insert/extract and scalar-result families would shrink the block substantially and fits the code's own idiom, so it would plausibly be accepted.

eval_const_int_expr_with_enums is a match over Expr, but two arms are self-contained computations with narrow inputs: the BinaryOp arm nests a 50-line match over BinOp with four near-identical signed/unsigned relational branches (Lt, Le, Gt, Ge), and the Cast arm carries 35 lines of width truncation and sign extension. Extracting fold_binop(op, l, r, unsigned) and a truncate-to-type helper is mechanical, removes the relational duplication, and leaves the top-level match as a readable dispatcher. Such a refactor would plausibly be accepted.

eval_const_int_expr_with_enums inlines a 55-line BinaryOp table in which the Lt/Le/Gt/Ge arms repeat the same unsigned-versus-signed comparison four times, and a 33-line Cast arm that implements width truncation with sign or zero extension. Both pieces are self-contained and can be extracted as helpers (an int binop evaluator taking an unsigned flag, and a truncate-to-type helper). lower_cast is a sequence of independent early-return cases: complex-to/from-real casts, the GCC cast-to-union extension with alloca and memcpy, cast-to-struct passthrough, vector-to-scalar, scalar-to-vector, vector-to-vector, then the scalar path with _Bool normalization. lower_cast is a chain of independent early-return blocks: complex casts, a 30-line cast to a union type that allocates, zero-inits and stores or memcpys, a struct pass-through, and three vector-cast blocks that each allocate and copy, before the scalar cast. The complex cases already delegate to real_to_complex and complex_to_complex, but the union and vector cases remain inline even though they share no state with the rest. Extracting lower_union_cast and lower_vector_cast follows that existing pattern and would plausibly be accepted.

lower_local_struct_init interleaves anonymous-member drilling, complex-field memcpy, struct-from-sret copies, char-array string literals, array-of-struct flat initializers and scalar-array flat initializers in one loop nested five levels deep, mutating item_idx from several branches. The array-field cases (lines 736 to 815) are separable into a helper that returns the number of items consumed, the same contract emit_struct_init already uses in this branch, and the anonymous-member and complex-field cases extract the same way. Decomposition is feasible and would make the item-consumption logic auditable.

lower_local_struct_init nests up to seven levels inside a manual item_idx loop: anonymous-member drilling, complex fields, and then an Expr arm that splits into struct memcpy, char-array string copy, array-of-structs flat consumption, and scalar-array flat consumption, each mutating item_idx. The array branches (about 70 lines) are separable helpers that would return the number of items consumed, a pattern emit_struct_init already uses. Decomposition is feasible and would plausibly be accepted given how hard the current nesting is to follow.

simplify_binop computes a few operand facts (lhs_zero, rhs_one, same_value, is_float) and then runs one flat match over IrBinOp whose arms are lists of algebraic identities, each commented and each returning a rewritten Instruction; the heavier rewrites are already delegated to try_reassociate_*, try_mul_power_of_two and const_power_of_two. Splitting per opcode would push the same seven inputs and precomputed facts into a dozen functions without separating any responsibility, so the flat rule table is the clearest available form. A minimal crate with a long peephole-style match over an operator enum whose arms are short early-return rules could reproduce this as a regression seed.

simplify_binop is one match over IrBinOp in which every arm is a short, flat list of algebraic identities (x+0, x*1, x&0, x|all_ones, x^x and similar), each one commented. The nontrivial rewrites are already factored out into try_reassociate_add/sub/mul/bitwise/shift and try_mul_power_of_two. Its length comes from the number of operators covered, not from nesting or coupling, and reading it as one identity table is the clearest form, so splitting it into per-operator functions would scatter the table without simplifying anything. A minimal crate with a long function made of one top-level match whose many arms are shallow and independent reproduces this, so it can serve as a regression seed.

MdrApp::ui runs five distinct phases in one body: reloading the file on watcher events, F10/Ctrl+F/Escape key handling, the search bar panel with match navigation, the TOC side panel, and the central scroll area. MdrApp::ui runs five distinct phases in one body: reload on watcher change, keyboard shortcut handling, a 90-line search bar panel with match navigation, the TOC side panel, and the central content render. Each phase touches a clear subset of fields (search_* for the search bar, toc_* for the TOC panel), so extracting reload_if_changed, show_search_bar and show_toc_panel is the usual egui structure. adjudication.criterion: A finding is a true positive when the flagged site should actually be changed, judged at the pinned revision under the published scope of the rule; it is a false positive when the flagged construct is correct as written, when its safety is established by the surrounding code, or when the context makes the flagged behaviour the intended one. Confirming that the rule's pattern is present is a separate, mechanical check: it proves the span is not corrupted, never that the site is a defect. For structural findings the value question is stated separately. A duplication family is a true positive when its members repeat a nontrivial shared scaffold that one definition, parameter or macro could serve without changing behavior; it is a false positive when the shared body is a short delegation whose entire difference lives in the erased names, when the members mirror each other by design, as benchmark or test comparison pairs and replays under a different harness do, or when separate trait impls the language forces apart leave nothing to factor. A complexity or size hotspot is a true positive when decomposition is feasible and would plausibly be accepted, a false positive when the measured branch count or length is the clearest available form or is forced by a trait contract. An unreasoned allow or an unreferenced feature is a false positive when the surrounding code or manifest already documents the intent the detector could not read.
adjudication.provenance: Who produced each verdict. "human" names a site a person read and judged. "agent" names a site adjudicated by an agent under the published protocol: the site read in the pinned source with its surrounding code, blind to any prior verdict, with a disagreement between independent passes escalated rather than settled by the agent. "unrecorded" names the sites judged before this field existed, whose author is not established; they are published as they were measured rather than reattributed after the fact. A rate mixing provenances is worth its weakest one, and no verdict, whoever produced it, is certified beyond the agreement two trained reviewers reach with each other.

reviewed.justification: A build script has no caller to return an error to: its main returns unit, and terminating the process is how Cargo is told the build failed.

Read emit_alloca_aligned_addr_impl at 457 to 464 beside emit_alloca_aligned_addr_to_acc_impl at 466 to 474 in src/backend/i686/codegen/memory.rs: both read alloca_over_align, take the slot reference, then leal, addl align minus one and andl the negated alignment.
